problem: Test whether a shorter week could keep services running and improve wellbeing.
title: Iceland trials a shorter working week for public workers with no pay cut
actor_name: Reykjavik City Council and the Icelandic government
context: Trade unions and civil society groups campaigned for shorter hours.
decision_made: Move about 2,500 public-sector workers from 40 hours to 35 or 36 hours at the same pay.
action_taken: Trials ran from 2015, with shorter and more focused meetings among the main changes.
observed_outcome: Productivity stayed the same or improved in most workplaces, staff reported less stress and better work-life balance, and unions later renegotiated contracts so that about 86 percent of the workforce moved or gained the right to request shorter hours.
lessons: Public-sector trials with union backing can lead to broad adoption when output holds.
limitations: The findings come from researchers involved with the trials, not an independent evaluation. Timelines differ by source (2015 to 2017 or 2019). A later study reported lower uptake figures.

claims.claim_text: Iceland moved about 2,500 public-sector workers to a 35 or 36 hour week at the same pay.
Productivity stayed the same or improved in most workplaces and staff reported less stress.
